chief_complaint: progressive difficulty climbing stairs, frequent falls, calf enlargement, and using hands to push up off floor in 4-year-old boy
hpi_details: 4M presenting with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty climbing stairs and frequent falls, noted calf enlargement, and using his hands to push up off the floor (Gower sign) when rising.
ideas: She thinks her son has severe flat feet or tight leg muscles that are making him clumsy and prone to tripping.
concerns: She is worried that his legs are getting weaker and that he will be left behind or bullied when he starts preschool.
expectations: She hopes to get a referral for physical therapy and a prescription for supportive shoe inserts to help him walk better.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Duchenne muscular dystrophy evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming the diagnosis with CK and dystrophin gene testing before referral to a multidisciplinary neuromuscular team, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive difficulty climbing stairs, frequent falls, calf enlargement, and using hands to push up off floor in 4-year-old boy

Key HPI features: 4M with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty climbing stairs and frequent falls, noted calf enlargement, and using his hands to push up off the floor (Gower sign) when rising.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal for age. Waddling gait, positive Gower sign, firm calf pseudohypertrophy, and symmetric proximal muscle weakness (hip and shoulder girdle greater than distal) with diminished but present deep tendon reflexes. No sensory deficit. Cognitive, cardiac, and respiratory exam grossly normal but require baseline assessment.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Becker muscular dystrophy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Gower sign (using hands to push up from floor).
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with serum creatine kinase (markedly elevated) and dystrophin gene testing (deletion/duplication analysis, sequencing if needed), reserving muscle biopsy for inconclusive genetic results

Refer to a multidisciplinary neuromuscular team: pediatric neurology, cardiology (baseline and serial echocardiogram/ECG for cardiomyopathy), pulmonology, physical therapy, and orthopedics for contracture/scoliosis surveillance
Discuss early corticosteroid therapy, which can slow functional decline, per current DMD care guidelines
Provide genetic counseling to the family given X-linked recessive inheritance and carrier-testing implications for female relatives.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: 4-year-old boy with progressive difficulty climbing stairs, frequent falls, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a positive Gower sign.
red_flags: Gower sign (using hands to push up from floor)

must_ask.objective: Ask about how he gets up from the floor
must_ask.say: When he gets up from sitting on the floor, does he use his hands to push up his legs?
Have you noticed his calf muscles look unusually large or firm?

must_ask.objective: Ask about fall frequency and stair difficulty
must_ask.say: How often does he fall, and does he have trouble with stairs?
Does anyone else in the family, especially on the mother's side, have muscle weakness?

must_ask.objective: Explain the need for genetic and CK testing
must_ask.say: We need to check a blood muscle enzyme level and likely genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis.

history.answer: My 4-year-old son has been having trouble climbing stairs and keeps falling down a lot lately.
It is definitely real muscle weakness; he doesn't complain of any numbness, tingling, or odd sensations.
The weakness is mainly in both of his hips and thighs, and a bit in his shoulders, rather than his hands or feet.
We first started noticing it around 6 months ago, and it has been getting worse very gradually.
It has steadily gotten worse over time; he trips more often and needs more help getting around.
He walks with a waddling side-to-side gait, cannot jump, and has a very hard time going up stairs without pulling himself up.
He gets more fatigued after running or walking longer distances, but it doesn't fluctuate between morning and evening.
When he gets up from the carpet, he turns over, puts his hands on the ground, and uses his hands to push on his knees and thighs to stand up.
His calf muscles look unusually large and bulky like a little bodybuilder, but they feel quite firm rather than strong.
He trips and falls several times every single day, especially if he tries to walk quickly or climb a curb.
No, he has never complained of neck pain, back pain, or pain shooting into his arms or legs.
No, his speech is completely clear, his face looks symmetric, and he swallows food and liquids without choking.
No, he has had no shortness of breath, chewing problems, droopy eyelids, or double vision.
No, he is fully potty-trained and has had no bladder or bowel accidents or loss of sensation.
We have not seen any twitching or fluttering in his muscles.
No, he did not have a stomach flu, cold, or fever before this weakness began.
He was born healthy with no high blood pressure, diabetes, heart defects, or stroke history.
No, he has never taken steroids, diuretics, chemotherapy, or any nerve-damaging medications.

I thought maybe he just has flat feet or tight tendons that are making him clumsy and having trouble standing up. I'm really worried that his legs are actually losing strength and that he won't be able to run and play with the other children at preschool.
I was hoping you could refer us to physical therapy and prescribe some special shoe inserts to help him keep his balance.
He has no history of chronic medical conditions or previous illnesses.
He has never had any surgeries and has never been hospitalized.
He is not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
He has no known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
He was born at 39 weeks via normal vaginal delivery without any birth complications.
He walked slightly late at around 16 months, but he has been growing well along the normal growth curves.
All of his childhood vaccinations are completely up to date according to schedule.
He attends preschool on weekdays and no other children in his class have similar symptoms.
He lives at home with my husband, me, and his 7-year-old sister; no one smokes in the house.
Not applicable for a 4-year-old child; no secondhand smoke exposure at home.
My maternal uncle had severe muscle weakness and ended up using a wheelchair as a young boy, but my husband's side is healthy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable, well-nourished 4-year-old boy in no acute distress; noticeably enlarged calves.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact bilaterally; no facial droop, normal extraocular movements without ptosis, and normal tongue and palate movement.
Symmetric proximal muscle weakness with hip flexors and abductors 4/5 and shoulder abductors 4/5; distal strength is intact at 5/5; positive Gower sign when rising from floor.
Bilateral calf pseudohypertrophy, firm and nontender on palpation without warmth or erythema.
Bilateral patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes are diminished (1+); biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are 1+; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally (Babinski negative).
Normal sensation to light touch and pinprick symmetrically across all four extremities and trunk.
Waddling gait with lumbar hyperlordosis and toe walking; unable to run or jump smoothly; Romberg test is negative.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or signs of respiratory distress.
Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1 and S2, no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Height and weight at the 50th percentile for age; gross motor delay noted with intact fine motor and social milestones.
